indicators.note: crossing here is read as cross-wise, so the letters of the mountain range are crossed over into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, the anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A vehicle of old was taken over the Andes mountains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crossing' looks like a journey over the mountains, but it signals the letters of ANDES rearranged; 'used' joins the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A covered chair carried on poles by two bearers was a common way to travel in the 17th and 18th centuries.

indicators.note: going round about suggests the letters of the word are sent along a new, twisting order

explanation.surface: Someone was sent the long way round to their destination.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the definition and the wordplay: 'in a roundabout way' tells you to rearrange ROUTED, and a journey routed indirectly is a diversion.
explanation.definitionFit: To divert a journey off the direct road is to send it by an indirect path, a diversion.

clue.text: In one sense the real thing, though spirit-like

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the run of words that follows, from the end of one word onwards

explanation.surface: Something seems truly genuine in one way, yet ghostly too.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters lie in 'sensE THE REAL'; 'one' and 'thing' are surface padding. The surface plays on 'the real thing' being the opposite of ghostly.
explanation.definitionFit: Something ethereal is airy and insubstantial, like a ghost or other disembodied being.

clue.text: New York's out West from these scattered islands

indicators.note: being out means being absent, so the letter for this compass point is removed from the city's letters
the letters are strewn about into a new order once the W has gone

parts.note: the city's name with its possessive S, all used as letters

explanation.surface: The American city is absent from the west of a remote group of islands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' says the W (West) leaves NEWYORKS; 'scattered' rearranges the remaining NEYORKS. The Orkneys are an island group off the north coast of Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: The Orkneys are an archipelago north of the Scottish mainland, a group of islands.

indicators.note: in a down clue the second piece sits below the first, so this signals the order

parts.note: the M1 is Britain's best-known motorway, written here with the figure one as the letter I
stress is strain or tension

explanation.surface: A female driving teacher is getting anxious on the motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is the main motorway from London to the north of England; crosswords write it as MI. In this down clue 'under' puts STRESS below it.
explanation.definitionFit: A schoolmistress is a woman who teaches, so a mistress is a female teacher.

clue.text: Little chap, you could say, ready to fight at short notice

definitions.text: ready to fight at short notice

explanation.surface: A small fellow is described as always prepared for a scrap.
explanation.walkthrough: The first reading splits the answer as 'minute man', a tiny chap. Minutemen were American colonial militia pledged to turn out at a minute's warning.
explanation.definitionFit: Minute means tiny, so a minute man is a small fellow; colonial militiamen sworn to muster instantly were called that.

clue.text: Kind of work giving one little standing …

definitions.text: Kind of work giving one little standing

parts.words: Kind of work giving one little standing
parts.note: a desk job keeps you seated all day, so you hardly ever stand; standing also teases as status

explanation.surface: A lowly kind of job offers its holder scant status.
explanation.walkthrough: 'little standing' looks like low status, but read literally it means very little time on your feet: a seated job.
explanation.definitionFit: Desk-bound work involves sitting most of the time, with little physical movement.

parts.note: a protest occupying a building, where people stay seated to make a point, continuing the previous clue

explanation.surface: Following on, a protest that occupies a place shows how little standing there is.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue continues 7: protesters who occupy premises and refuse to move demonstrate a seated kind of activity. 'occupation' means a job in the surface and a protest takeover in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A protest in which people occupy a place and stay seated is both an occupation and a demonstration.

clue.text: Linen, not 26, in the crudest form

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the words that follow, running from the end of one into the next

explanation.surface: Unbleached cloth is the roughest version of the fabric.
explanation.walkthrough: 26 is BLEACHED, so 'Linen, not 26' is unbleached linen, and that colour is the definition. The letters lie in 'thE CRUdest'; 'form' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Ecru is the greyish-beige colour of linen left in its natural, untreated state.

clue.text: Jean astride a horse in James I's time

indicators.note: the name sits with its legs either side, surrounding the letters that follow

parts.note: taken as written
a cob is a sturdy short-legged horse

explanation.surface: A woman named Jean rides a horse in the early seventeenth century.
explanation.walkthrough: 'astride' pictures a rider with legs either side of the mount, so the name wraps the horse. Jacobean comes from Jacobus, Latin for James.
explanation.definitionFit: Jacobean describes the reign of James I of England, from Jacobus, the Latin form of his name.

explanation.surface: Someone clips an article from the newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: Both the noun and the verb fit: you snip a press item out, and the result is a clipping.
explanation.definitionFit: To cut out is to snip something free, and a cutout is a shape clipped from newspaper or card.

clue.text: Fish a senior fellow takes to heart

indicators.note: the letters lie at the centre of the phrase, held in its heart

explanation.surface: An elderly academic is emotionally attached to a fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes to heart' sounds like being moved, but it signals letters inside 'seniOR FEllow'.
explanation.definitionFit: The orfe, or ide, is a freshwater fish of the carp family, often golden in ornamental ponds.

clue.text: The answer to what may happen tomorrow

definitions.text: The answer to what may happen tomorrow

parts.words: The answer to what may happen tomorrow
parts.note: the stock reply when asked to predict the future: nobody knows

explanation.surface: Someone asks what tomorrow holds and gets the usual reply.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is a question in disguise; the stock reply admits the future is unknowable.
explanation.definitionFit: The saying expresses that the future is unpredictable, a natural reply to a question about tomorrow.

clue.text: Their love affairs appear below average

definitions.text: Their love affairs appear below average

indicators.note: in this down clue the second piece is placed beneath the first

parts.note: par is the normal or average level
amours are love affairs

explanation.surface: Their romances are rather substandard.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines too: lovers are those whose love affairs these are. In this down entry 'appear below' puts AMOURS under PAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Illicit lovers are the people whose romances these are.

indicators.note: fashioning means shaping anew, so the letters are made into a new form

parts.note: the word with its possessive S, all used as letters
taken as written

explanation.surface: A lout's headgear is trendy in the Moroccan city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fez' looks like the Moroccan city; it is the hat. 'fashionable' rearranges BOORS and HAT.
explanation.definitionFit: A fez is the brimless tasselled cap of the Near East, a kind of the felt cap called by this Arabic name.

clue.text: Plainly blessed cathedral city Welsh Jane is attached to

indicators.note: the second name is fastened on after the first, giving the order

parts.note: Ely is a small cathedral city in Cambridgeshire
Sian is the Welsh form of the name Jane

explanation.surface: A Welsh woman named Jane plainly loves a cathedral city.
explanation.walkthrough: ELY, a cathedral city in Cambridgeshire, England, then SIAN, the Welsh Jane. 'Plainly blessed' refers to the Elysian plains or fields of the blessed dead.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the Elysian Fields were the plains where the virtuous dead dwelt in bliss.

clue.text: Strike the flag at a Welsh university

parts.note: to lam is to hit hard
the Blue Peter is a signal flag hoisted when a ship is about to sail

explanation.surface: Someone lowers the flag at a university in Wales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strike the flag' means lower it in surrender, but here LAM (hit) plus PETER, from the Blue Peter signal flag. Lampeter is a small Welsh university town.
explanation.definitionFit: Lampeter, in Ceredigion, has the oldest degree-awarding institution in Wales, St David's College.

explanation.surface: Traditional cricketers from the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: The Derby is one of the five English horse-racing Classics; in America a bowler hat is a derby. 'bowlers' looks like cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: Races named after the Epsom original count among the Classics, and Americans call the hard felt bowler hat a derby.

parts.note: fair means reasonable or just
a game is a match

explanation.surface: Someone has found a sensible partner for their aunt.
explanation.walkthrough: Aunt Sally is a British pub game of throwing sticks at a dummy's head, and so anyone set up as a target of criticism. 'match' suggests a partner.
explanation.definitionFit: An Aunt Sally is a target of ridicule, someone it is acceptable to attack or mock.

explanation.surface: A breezy room is the same thing as a ghostly one.
explanation.walkthrough: 3 is ETHEREAL, of which this is a synonym: insubstantial, light as the breeze.
explanation.definitionFit: Fresh-aired rooms let the breeze through, and something light and insubstantial is also described as this.

explanation.surface: A society that supplies a little seasoning.
explanation.walkthrough: A mace is a heavy club, and also the spice made from the outer covering of the nutmeg.
explanation.definitionFit: A spiked heavy staff is a weapon of war, and the dried nutmeg aril is a cooking spice.

clue.text: Suffering in court puts the seal on it

indicators.note: the pain is set inside the abbreviation

parts.note: an ache is pain or suffering

explanation.surface: Pain endured at a hearing settles the matter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts the pain inside the court. A cachet was originally a seal on a letter; 'puts the seal on it' sounds like finishing something off.
explanation.definitionFit: A cachet is a distinguishing stamp or mark, originally a seal affixed to a document.

parts.note: a length of river between two bends, and also to extend, as of an arm

explanation.surface: A length of river between bends.
explanation.walkthrough: The word means both to stretch out and a straight length of river.
explanation.definitionFit: On a river, the straight length between two bends is called by this name.

clue.text: Anguish of a buck, we hear

indicators.note: the word for the money is spoken, giving a sound like a different word

parts.note: a buck is slang for a dollar

explanation.surface: A male deer seems to be in great distress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'buck' looks like a deer, but it is a dollar; 'we hear' gives a word sounding like it.
explanation.definitionFit: Dolour is a poetic word for sorrow or grief, deep distress of mind.

parts.note: literally washed until white rather than covered up, a scandal hushed

explanation.surface: Was the scandal covered up?
explanation.walkthrough: Whitewash usually means a cover-up; read literally it is something washed white with chemicals.
explanation.definitionFit: Linen treated with chemicals until it turns white has been washed white.

parts.note: an irritable comment pairs with a note about crossings, since zebra crossings are British road crossings

explanation.surface: Someone writes an irritable remark about striped animals.
explanation.walkthrough: Peevish gives CROSS and a note gives REFERENCE, but the clue pictures a note about zebra crossings, the British striped pedestrian crossings: a reference to crossings.
explanation.definitionFit: A note directing the reader to another place in a text is this kind of pointer.
